1.pericope_label: Let not your heart be troubled

schools.summary: Gill enumerates the causes of the trouble; Calvin points past them to faith in Christ as the Son of God, and defends the received reading of the first clause.
Henry weighs the emphasis on each word and takes the first clause as acknowledgement, the second as command.

Ellicott ties the words to the preceding scene and reads both clauses as imperatives; Robertson locates the heart as the seat of spiritual life; Lightfoot diagnoses a national disappointment; Barnes sets the scene at the supper.
Clarke reads the verse as the answer continued to Peter’s question; Wesley makes believing the sum of the whole discourse.
Both Augustinian excerpts ground the consolation in Christ’s divinity: the command to believe in him follows from belief in God only if he is God.

debates.question: Is the first clause indicative (ye believe in God) or imperative (believe in God)?

sides.position: Both clauses imperative
First indicative, second imperative — the received reading

outliers.note: Alone in tracing the disciples’ distress to the specific expectation of a restored national kingdom and the reproach they had met instead.

2.pericope_label: In my Father’s house are many mansions

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the mansions as room enough for all rather than ranks of honour; Calvin also uses the verse to settle the state of the fathers before the ascension.
Ellicott traces the word through Vulgate and early English versions; Robertson parses the unfulfilled condition; Lightfoot and Barnes supply the ark and the universe-as-house images.
Clarke reads many mansions as graded glory matched to capacity; Wesley reads it only as sufficiency of room.

debates.question: Do the many mansions mean differing degrees of glory?

sides.position: Yes, degrees suited to capacity and attainment
No — only sufficiency of room; the saints’ glory is one
Varying happiness is implied but is not the thought here

debates.question: What is the coming again of v.3?

sides.position: His constant spiritual presence, completed in final union
The last day, when he comes to gather his followers

outliers.note: Suggests the Father’s house is the whole universe, earth and heaven alike being mansions in it, so that death is a move between apartments of one dwelling.

4.pericope_label: And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know

schools.summary: Gill allows them only a confused and imperfect knowledge; Calvin reads the verse as proof that the death is a passage, and that the disciples must travel the same road.
Henry hears both a permission and a fact in ye know, and takes Christ to credit his people with more knowledge than they can feel in themselves.

Barnes and Robertson hold the way was already plain from repeated warning; Ellicott prefers a joined reading, whither I go, ye know the way, and contrasts what they ought to have known with what they did.
Clarke says the teaching had been plain enough to be comprehended; Wesley defines the way as faith, holiness and sufferings.
Augustine of Hippo identifies the mansions with the believers themselves, prepared by the purifying of their hearts while Christ is away.

debates.question: How far did the disciples already know the way?

sides.position: They truly knew it, though not under that description
Only confusedly and imperfectly
They had been told plainly and could not but have understood
They ought to have known; the means lay within reach, and the saying exposes the gap

outliers.note: Makes the preparing of the mansions and the sanctifying of the disciples one act, since the dwellers are themselves the dwelling.

5.pericope_label: Thomas asks the way; I am the way, the truth, and the life

schools.summary: Gill insists Christ is the way of salvation itself, not merely its example or herald; Calvin finds three degrees and defends Thomas from the charge of contradiction.

Ellicott contrasts Thomas’s whither with Christ’s way and makes the pronoun emphatic; Robertson names Thomas the materialist; Barnes blames prejudice; Lightfoot sets the saying against the Jewish estimate of the law.
Wesley matches each title to one of the questions raised; Clarke subdivides the way and the truth.
Chrysostom reads the question as the anxiety of love; Cyril of Jerusalem turns the closing clause against any approach to the Father that bypasses the Son.
Origen treats the saying as one instance of the many names of good things under which the Son is announced.
Augustine reads the three as whereby, whereto and wherein, and makes the incarnation the making of the way.

debates.question: Why are truth and life added when the question was only about the way?

sides.position: A Hebrew idiom for the true and living way, and a polemic against the law
Each title answers a separate question Thomas had raised
They mark beginning, middle and end of one course
Whereby, whereto, and wherein — the road, the destination and the abiding

outliers.note: Reads the verse less as a definition than as an enumeration, adding the resurrection and the door to the list of names by which the Son is preached.

themes: the exclusive way to the Father

7.pericope_label: If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also

schools.summary: Gill grants them real but partial knowledge; Calvin makes the fault a refusal to acknowledge the Father’s image already exhibited before their eyes.
Ellicott and Robertson read the deficiency out of the Greek verbs — recognition rather than acquaintance; Barnes and Lightfoot trace it instead to inherited Jewish expectation.
Clarke grounds the inference both in the unity of Father and Son and in the true design of the law.
Augustine of Hippo reads the verse by the promise before it and finds the disciples’ destination to be Christ himself, who is the life he possesses.

debates.question: In what sense had the disciples not known Christ?

sides.position: They had not recognised who he is; the Greek distinguishes observation from reflection
Their knowledge was real but partial, hemmed in by expectation of a temporal Messiah
They failed to acknowledge the fullness of the Godhead manifested in him

outliers.note: Explains the disciples’ dullness historically, as the second temple’s traditions doubling an obscurity the first temple already had.

themes: knowing the Father in the Son

8.pericope_label: Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us

schools.summary: Gill sees a reverent confession of ignorance; Calvin charges the apostles’ fault against every later reader.

Ellicott, Lightfoot and Robertson read the request as a hope for a visible theophany on the model of Moses; Barnes replies that sufficient evidence had already been given in the works and words of Christ.
Clarke partly excuses Philip, who had not witnessed the transfiguration and expected a new manifestation to accompany a new law.
John Chrysostom holds Philip did want bodily sight, explains why he asked at this moment, and guards the answer against confusing the two persons.
Hilary denies that Philip wanted bodily sight at all, and takes the reproof to be that the divine nature was not discerned through the assumed humanity.

debates.question: What kind of showing did Philip ask for?

sides.position: A visible manifestation of glory, like the one given to Moses
Not bodily sight, but that the Father already seen in the Son be made plain to the understanding

outliers.note: Declines to treat the apostles’ slowness as a historical curiosity, applying every fault in the scene directly to the reader.

9.pericope_label: He that hath seen me hath seen the Father

schools.summary: Gill lists the proofs already given; Calvin traces Philip’s blindness to ingratitude and to a distaste for Christ’s low condition.

Ellicott hears sadness in the question and applies it to any long familiarity that never became recognition; Barnes measures the three years of evidence and defines what seeing God can mean; Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun.
Clarke takes the saying as a bare claim to deity that no creature could make.
Cyril of Jerusalem states the likeness of Son to Father in full and guards it equally against separating the persons and against confusing them.

debates.question: What is meant by seeing the Father in the Son?

sides.position: A manifestation from which God’s character is learned — never his invisible essence
The unchanged characteristics of Godhead beheld in the Son, so that beholding him is fruition of the Father
The Father present in Christ, missed only through ingratitude and distaste for his low condition

outliers.note: Treats Philip’s request as a standing modern demand and answers it as such, rather than only as a first-century question.

10.pericope_label: I am in the Father, and the Father in me

schools.summary: Calvin refers the saying to the manner of revelation and to power rather than essence, while granting the fathers’ use of it for Christ’s divinity; Gill notes a variant reading the clause as a question.

Ellicott reads the words as the whole revelation of the Father and prefers the reading that the indwelling Father does his own works; Barnes measures the union against what a mere prophet could have said; Robertson notes the renewed appeal to believe.
Clarke and Wesley take the oneness as one of essence as well as operation, and Wesley locates the proof in the manner of the miracles rather than their bare occurrence.
Cyril of Jerusalem holds the wording to its exact form as a guard against both separating and confusing the persons.
Augustine of Hippo counts the words themselves as works and grounds the saying in the Son’s being God of God.

debates.question: Does the mutual indwelling speak of essence or of revelation and power?

sides.position: Of the manner of revelation and of power, not of the hidden essence
Of essence as well as operation
Of a union closer than any prophet could claim, shown in the works
Of an ordered relation — God of God — neither separate nor confused

outliers.note: Locates the evidential force of the miracles not in the acts but in the sovereign manner of their performance.

12.pericope_label: He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also

schools.summary: Gill confines the promise to the apostles; Calvin explains why it was needed and finds its fulfilment in the conversion of the world after the ascension.
Henry takes the promise as armour against the disciples’ fear of abandonment, and as a further proof of the power that could delegate itself.
Barnes and Robertson deny that the works are greater in power and locate the excess in effect and in quantity; Ellicott widens the promise to the whole history of the Church.
Clarke and Wesley catalogue the apostolic miracles and then rank the conversion of one sinner above them all.
Chrysostom reads the works as words whose fruit is faith, and refuses to narrow the promise to the apostles.

debates.question: To whom is the promise made?

sides.position: The apostles only
Every believer, the promise resting on faith itself

debates.question: In what sense are the works greater?

sides.position: Greater in effect and extent, not in power
Greater in quantity, not in quality
Greater as preaching, whose fruit is faith
Greater in the conversion of sinners above any miracle
Greater as the whole subsequent work of the Church

outliers.note: Explains the promise from human forgetfulness rather than from apostolic office, arguing the clause exists because a fortnight’s silence from God makes us doubt he is alive.

13.pericope_label: Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do

schools.summary: Gill takes the promise as unrestricted in subject; Calvin reads it as a statement of Christ’s mediatorial office and of the hallowing of God’s name in him.

Barnes explains the name by analogies of authorised petition; Ellicott makes the phrase itself the limit on whatsoever; Robertson notes that the Son answers prayer here and defends the reading ask me.
Clarke confines the promise to what the mission required, and connects it with the sending of the Spirit.

debates.question: What limits the word whatsoever?

sides.position: The phrase in my name; personal petitions only as they glorify God, and refusal may be the truest answer
Faith and conformity to God’s will
Nothing in the subject matter — any blessing, for themselves or others
The apostolic commission it was given to serve

debates.question: Why is the promise repeated in v.14?

sides.position: An emphatic repetition, the stress now on the pronoun
To confirm the disciples’ faith — against those who think the words came in from a margin
To teach direct prayer to Christ, if the reading ask me is genuine
To stop us seeking other intercessors

outliers.note: Reads unanswered prayer as itself a form of answer, and treats the customary closing formula of Christian prayer as a request for exactly that.

themes: prayer in the name of Christ

15.pericope_label: If ye love me, keep my commandments; another Comforter

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take Christ to be speaking as Mediator, Calvin correcting a love that wished to keep him in the world and reconciling his obtaining the Spirit with his giving him.
Henry reads the clause as duty set inside consolation, and makes the day’s duty swallow up care about the day’s events.

Barnes tests love by obedience and refers the praying to the ascended intercession; Robertson and Ellicott work from the Greek of the condition and of the title; Lightfoot recovers the Jewish expectation behind Comforter.
Clarke unfolds the full range of the word and distinguishes the two advocacies; Wesley presses another and for ever.
John Chrysostom and Chrysostom tie the commandment to the promise before it and define love as obedience rather than grief; Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the Spirit’s titles into one identity.
Bede derives the double procession from the two titles; Augustine of Hippo attends to the manner in which the promise was given.

debates.question: Is the promised one best called Comforter or Advocate?

sides.position: Advocate is the better rendering
Comforter suits the disciples’ distress and their nation’s expectation
The word carries both and more — counsellor, patron, mediator

debates.question: Does Christ obtain the Spirit or bestow him?

sides.position: Both — as Mediator he obtains, as God he bestows
He speaks here strictly as Mediator, interceding
The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son alike

outliers.note: Reads the title against the rabbinic name Menahem for the Messiah, so that the promise answers an expectation the disciples already carried.

17.pericope_label: Even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive

schools.summary: Gill identifies the Spirit as the author of Scripture and the giver of boldness; Calvin makes the world’s incapacity a measure of the gift and confines it to the elect.

Barnes and Robertson describe a world that walks by sight and lacks spiritual faculty; Ellicott states the principle and reads the disciples’ present possession from the better text; Lightfoot supplies the historical setting of falsehood the title answers.
Clarke traces unbelief to appetites that admit only what the senses report; Wesley reduces the office to four verbs and makes the indwelling a permanent tenancy.

debates.question: Why can the world not receive the Spirit?

sides.position: It walks by sight, and what the senses cannot register makes no impression
It has lost the spiritual faculty by which alone he could be received
The gift is a special grace given to the elect, and the exclusion measures its worth

outliers.note: Insists that the neuter relative agreeing with the word for spirit must still be rendered whom, since a person and not an influence is promised.

18.pericope_label: I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you

schools.summary: Gill reads Christ as father to his people; Calvin makes the verse a lesson in helplessness without the Spirit, and finds in it the mode of Christ’s omnipresence.
Henry hears the idiom of parting friends and insists the departure was neither total nor final.
Ellicott and Robertson correct the rendering to orphans; Ellicott refers the coming to the Paraclete, Barnes to a series of returns.
Clarke supplies the etymologies and the rabbinic custom that gives the image its force; Wesley notes the word belongs to bereavement.

Augustine guards Christ’s own presence alongside the Spirit’s and limits the manner of the return; Augustine of Hippo qualifies the fatherhood carefully; Hilary adds the sacrament as a mode of indwelling.

debates.question: What is the promised coming?

sides.position: The spiritual presence in the person of the Paraclete
The resurrection first of all
Both the resurrection and the later gift of the Spirit
A real return, but not the old daily presence, and to his own only

outliers.note: Introduces the eucharist as the means by which Christ is in his disciples, a mode none of the other witnesses raises here.

19.pericope_label: Because I live, ye shall live also

schools.summary: Gill limits the world’s sight of Christ to the bodily and the judgment; Calvin substitutes the eyes of faith, makes Christ’s life the cause of ours, and stretches that day to the last resurrection.

Barnes dates the saying and grounds the promise in a nature that could not die; Robertson makes the risen life the guarantee; Ellicott traces the education from physical to spiritual presence and reads the knowledge as the cry of adoption.
Clarke makes the resurrection both proof and pledge and adds the life of intercession; Wesley divides the promise by the two natures.

debates.question: What is that day?

sides.position: After the resurrection
The resurrection, but more eminently Pentecost
The whole new dispensation of the Spirit
Pentecost first, then every spiritual quickening and the last day
One unbroken day from the Spirit’s first working to the last resurrection

outliers.note: Denies the clause refers to the resurrection at all, resting it instead on a nature in Christ that could not die.

21.pericope_label: He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me

schools.summary: Gill requires the commandments written on the heart, not merely possessed in a text; Calvin defines having and keeping, defends the priority of God’s love, and makes growth in knowledge the reward of obedience.

Ellicott and Robertson read the verse as an ascending series ending in manifestation, and press the emphatic demonstrative; Barnes reads the same chain backwards as proof of a single kingdom bound by love.
Wesley glosses the having as inward and the manifesting as more abundant; Clarke splits the promise between the resurrection appearances and a manifestation lasting to the end of the world.

debates.question: Does the verse make our love the cause of the Father’s?

sides.position: No — no question of cause and effect is raised; the love of God is prior and is here only attested in the heart
The clauses describe successive degrees of receptivity, not an origin of love
They are evidences of a union already established between Father, Son and disciples

outliers.note: Turns the promise into a diagnosis of why so few advance, reckoning that scarcely one in ten proceeds in the right course.

themes: obedience as the test of love

22.pericope_label: Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?

schools.summary: Gill identifies the speaker with Jude the apostle; Calvin grants the force of the question and judges the answer to leave its deepest cause untouched.

Ellicott and Robertson trace the question to a Messianic expectation of public theophany and to the idiom what has happened that; Barnes attributes it instead to a narrower confusion about the resurrection.
Clarke supposes Judas expected a kingdom covering all the earth.
Augustine grounds the difference in love and in the house where Father and Son abide; Augustine of Hippo makes the scene a model of attentive reading.

debates.question: What did Judas expect instead?

sides.position: A public Messianic theophany, the manifestation being to a few appearing as a change of plan
Only the resurrection, which he could not see being private

debates.question: Does Christ’s reply answer the question asked?

sides.position: Yes — the difference is that some love him and some do not
Only in part — it passes over why any come to love him at all

outliers.note: Reads the passage as an invitation to join the questioning disciples rather than as a report of what they were told.

themes: the indwelling of Father and Son

23.pericope_label: If a man love me, he will keep my words; and we will come unto him

schools.summary: Calvin denies that God’s love follows ours in order of cause and confines the verse to love sealed on the heart; Gill applies the negative clause to hollow professors as well as to the profane.

Ellicott makes the verse the answer to Judas and traces the temple image through Scripture and Philo; Robertson presses the continuing condition and the plural coming; Barnes describes what the indwelling brings.
Clarke extends the promise to all later believers and makes the heart a temple; Wesley reads a proportion between obedience and the Father’s love.

debates.question: Does the Father’s love follow the disciple’s?

sides.position: It increases with obedience — the more a man loves, the more God loves him
No — God’s love is not in the second rank; the verse speaks of that love sealed on the heart, not of its origin

debates.question: Why can the world not receive the manifestation?

sides.position: It has closed the channels itself and has nothing receptive of the divine presence
It does not keep his words, whether by hollow observance or open neglect
It is justly left in its blindness for its ingratitude

outliers.note: Supports the image of the indwelt heart from a contemporary non-Christian writer as well as from the Old Testament sanctuary.

themes: the indwelling of Father and Son

25.pericope_label: The Comforter shall teach you all things

schools.summary: Gill itemises these things and weighs advocate against comforter; Calvin reads the verse as a remedy against discouragement at slow understanding.
Henry hears Christ ratifying his teaching and using his remaining time to the full, and turns it into a rule for hearers of departing teachers.

Ellicott and Robertson read the pause and the tenses, and both bound the promise by what Christ had already said; Barnes takes it as a promise of apostolic inspiration; Lightfoot restricts being led into all truth to the apostles alone.
Clarke makes the recollection exact enough to preserve the identical words; Wesley extends the promise to later believers so far as saving truth goes.
Cyril of Jerusalem joins the two verbs and shows from the Spirit’s recorded speech that he acts with authority as a person.
Augustine of Hippo distinguishes the bodily dwelling now ending from the spiritual dwelling promised, one that comes and goes from one that never withdraws.

debates.question: How far does teach you all things extend?

sides.position: To the apostles alone as regards truth for the whole church; to every believer as regards his own
To the apostles and their successors, so far as truth needful for salvation
To the apostolic office, covering the founding of the church and the recording of its truths
Bounded by the words Christ had already spoken to them

outliers.note: Sets two modes of divine dwelling side by side, arguing that the bodily one visits and departs while the spiritual one never withdraws.

27.pericope_label: Peace I leave with you; my Father is greater than I

schools.summary: Gill reads the peace as a testamentary legacy; Calvin distinguishes it from human wishes by its effect and refers the closing clause to Christ’s mediatorial descent rather than to either nature.
Henry grounds their calm in Christ’s own, and makes the parting a good night rather than a farewell.
Ellicott traces the greeting and then argues for a subordination within the divine nature; Robertson confines the comparison to rank; Barnes refers it to condition rather than nature.
Clarke sets the promised peace against salutations of mere custom and takes the Father to be greater as sender over sent; Wesley divides peace with God from the peace Christ himself enjoys.
Chrysostom hears farewell and consolation together and reads the encouragement as accommodation to the disciples’ weakness.
Origen likens the peace to the calm weather in which a house strong enough to survive the flood must be built.
Augustine of Hippo divides the departure between the nature bounded by place and the nature that is everywhere; Hilary argues that receiving unity from the giver does not make the receiver less.

debates.question: In what sense is the Father greater than the Son?

sides.position: As regards the Son’s human nature — a defence explicitly rejected
As sender is greater than sent
A subordination within the divine nature itself
In rank only, not in nature or essence
In condition — humiliation against the glory he resumes
Neither nature is in view: Christ stands between God and us to raise us
The giver is greater, but the one given unity is not thereby less

outliers.note: Answers the gift of peace with an architectural image rather than an exposition, making calm the precondition of any structure meant to last.

themes: the Father greater than the Son

29.pericope_label: I have told you before it come to pass; the prince of this world cometh

schools.summary: Gill reads the prediction as proof of omniscience and marks the shortening time; Calvin treats the foretelling as a concession to weakness and guards the devil’s title from dualism.

Barnes takes the prediction as evidence and explains why temptation had no purchase; Ellicott weighs two readings of the clause and presses the absoluteness of the denial; Robertson names the prince as Satan; Lightfoot gives the phrase its contemporary Jewish sense.
Clarke supplies both a pastoral motive and the textual variant, and reports rival identifications of the prince; Wesley reduces the denial to want of right, claim and power.
Augustine of Hippo objects that faith is praised for believing what it does not see, and doubts whether sight leaves room for belief at all.

debates.question: Who is the prince of this world?

sides.position: Satan, working here in and by Judas
The devil as ruler among the Gentiles, whose dominion is now contested
Christ himself, as the ruler who is coming
The Roman government, which by its deputy would judge him

debates.question: Why foretell the event at all?

sides.position: So that fulfilled prediction may confirm faith
So that the death may not be a stumbling-block and their grief be mitigated
As a concession, the event serving afterwards as interpreter of the doctrine

outliers.note: Presses the difficulty the promise creates for the nature of faith, since faith is commended precisely for resting on what is not seen.

schools.summary: Gill restricts the world to the elect; Calvin subordinates the whole scene to the decree of God and makes the non-resistance itself the ransom.

Ellicott repunctuates the verse as one sentence and reads the world’s knowledge as the defeat of its prince; Robertson supplies an ellipsis; Barnes and Lightfoot dispute where the following discourse was delivered.
Wesley puts the obedience in Christ’s own voice and locates the next chapters in the city; Clarke reports the road reconstruction with its hour and moon, and draws a rule for conduct.
John Chrysostom makes the summons an occasion to argue that courage and cowardice are matters of will, and rejects the suggestion that Christ moved out of fear.

debates.question: Where were the following chapters spoken?

sides.position: On the road from the supper room to Gethsemane
Still in the same room, the discourse running straight on
In the city after leaving Bethany, before crossing the brook

debates.question: How should the verse be punctuated?

sides.position: One sentence, everything before arise governed by that
A break, with a suppressed clause understood before the purpose
Either arrangement will serve; the sense is unaffected

outliers.note: Takes the world that is to know Christ’s love to mean the elect only, against the reading that makes it the world the prince of this world had ruled.
